I say someone post recently about adding this to their agents.md file, what do we think about that?

# MSW — the kernel

## program — complete

```
contract ← the requested outcome + the smallest criteria that prove it

while ∃ claim c : deleting c leaves contract unmet ∨ unproven
      do c ; prove c

halt ; report
```

## definitions — no behavior lives here, only meaning

**contract** — the requested outcome and the smallest set of acceptance criteria that would prove it, stated before any work. The sole source of necessity; a ceiling as much as a floor. If the request is ambiguous: attended → ask; unattended → bind the smallest reading consistent with stated intent and record the assumption.

**claim** — anything petitioning to become work: a plan step, a change, a test, a reviewer's P1, a discovered edge case, your own instinct that one more pass would help. Everything enters as this type. Nothing enters as a verdict.

**deleting c leaves contract unmet ∨ unproven** — the only test. A claim passes solely by breaking the contract — reproducibly, within the task's actual inputs and environment. Severity is derived from the contract, never inherited from whoever raised the claim. *Useful*, *thorough*, and *possible* are not aliases for *necessary*. A claim that fails receives one line in the report — never a fix, an investigation, or a deferred follow-up.

**do ; prove** — the smallest reliable act that closes the gap, and evidence sized to the claim it settles. An unproven act keeps its claim alive; a proven one closes it — and re-proving a closed claim is itself an inadmissible claim.

**halt** — the fixed point: contract proven, no remaining claim passes. Not reviewer silence; not exhausted imagination. Halting before the fixed point and looping past it are the same bug, mirrored.

**report** — the outcome against the contract; the proof; rejected claims worth the user's attention, one line each. Nothing else.

## fuses — outside the program, for when its evaluator fails

```
rounds = 3            → halt anyway ; report open items, do not chase them
claim born in round n+1, visible in round n   → rejected
```

## No unauthoritative limits

Never invent a limit. A cap, threshold, quota, budget, timeout, retry or round count, file or line count, acceptance-criterion count, agent count, or similar constraint is admissible only when its exact value is:

- explicitly required by the requester;
- imposed by an applicable technical or platform contract;
- defined by authoritative project policy; or
- derived from measured evidence necessary to meet or prove the task contract.

State the authority or derivation whenever proposing or applying a limit. If no authority exists, omit the limit and use the MSW necessity test. Metrics may be reported as evidence, but they must not become gates, defaults, targets, or recommendations through agent intuition. Examples and representative proportions never become defaults. If a necessary limit is an unresolved owner choice, ask; do not manufacture a value.

-----------------------------

Skip it as a paste-in. The diagnosis behind it is right, the artifact itself is worse than what you already run, and one or two lines are worth stealing.

**What it gets right**

It targets real agent failure modes: scope creep dressed up as thoroughness, endless polish loops, premature halting, and reviewer P1s treated as commands rather than claims to verify. The two sharpest ideas are the deletion test ("would removing this work leave the contract unmet?") and "everything enters as a claim, nothing enters as a verdict."

**Why I wouldn't add it**

The form fights the goal. Models don't execute pseudo-code — there is no evaluator running that while-loop. The `∃ claim c` register is written to impress readers of the post, and plain imperative instructions steer a model better per token than an invented formalism it has to interpret.

It contradicts itself. `rounds = 3` is precisely the invented, unauthorized limit its own final section bans. The "fuses live outside the program" dodge is the kind of cleverness a model applies inconsistently. Worse, the second fuse can reject a genuine contract-breaking bug just because it surfaced a round late — the deletion test says fix it, the fuse says drop it, and nothing says which wins.

The no-limits rule is too absolute. It is good against agents silently inventing "top 10" caps. It is hostile to ordinary judgment defaults — timeouts, retries, page sizes — and "ask, do not manufacture" is a stall in unattended runs.

You already have this. Your Product Contract and Scope sections cover contract-first work, proving at the closest real surface, and not expanding the boundary — in plainer language that also routes to your ce-* skills. Two overlapping doctrines in different registers create ambiguity about which one governs, which is its own instruction-following bug.

One more sharp edge: "a claim that fails receives one line — never a fix, an investigation, or a deferred follow-up" would suppress the "flagged but left alone" reporting you currently get, which I'd consider a loss.

**Worth stealing**

Two lines, translated into your file's plain style:

- Treat all incoming pressure to do work — reviewer comments, discovered edge cases, your own instinct for one more pass — as claims to test against the contract, with severity derived from the contract rather than from who raised it.
- Never invent numeric limits (caps, retries, thresholds, round counts); take them from the request, the platform, policy, or measurement, and name the source.

If you want, I can draft those two lines into `~/.agents/AGENTS.md` — but as written, MSW is a good blog post and a mediocre instruction file.

The poster claims it has really good effects on deleting the size of code written. I still think sometimes that A g agents using my setup still add too much code around edge cases that don't really deserve their place in the code. So I'm wondering if there's anything that we can steal from this that helps with deleting unnecessary code. Especially with tests. Tests are all over the place.

Yes — there are three mechanisms in MSW that plausibly explain the poster's "less code" effect, and all three translate into plain lines you can steal. The poster's claim is believable because the mechanism is real: MSW inverts the burden of proof so code must justify existing, instead of a reviewer justifying removal.

**Why your current setup doesn't catch this**

Your "smallest resulting system" line operates at architecture level. Your Scope section operates at workflow level. An agent adding a null-guard, a fallback branch, and six tests around a three-line change violates neither — it sees itself as careful, and nothing in the file tests each guard or test individually. The missing rule is granular.

**Steal — three rules, translated into your style**

1. The deletion test, applied per-line instead of per-task:

> Apply the deletion test to every guard, branch, fallback, and test: if deleting it would not make the task's proof fail, do not write it.

2. The reachability rule for edge cases (MSW: claims must break the contract "within the task's actual inputs and environment"):

> Handle an edge case only when a real caller or input in this system can produce it. Name that source. If you cannot name one, do not write the handler — give the rejected case one line in the report instead.

The "name that source" step is what does the work. It converts a vague instinct ("be robust") into a check the agent fails concretely.

3. Test admissibility (MSW: "evidence sized to the claim it settles" + "re-proving a closed claim is inadmissible"):

> Each new test must prove one acceptance criterion or reproduce one observed failure. Name which one.
> Do not add a test that proves what an existing test already proves.
> Test the promised behavior, not your implementation's branches.
> Extend the existing suite for the surface you changed. Create a new test file only when no suite covers that surface.

The last line targets your "tests all over the place" complaint directly — that's placement sprawl, which MSW doesn't address at all, so that one is mine, not stolen.

**One line for AGENTS.md itself**

The single best sentence in MSW for your problem, near-verbatim:

> The contract is a ceiling as much as a floor. Useful, thorough, and possible are not aliases for necessary.

**Where it goes**

Your AGENTS.md says the taste skills own code-shape rules, and `code-taste` already lists "speculative guards" as its territory. So the durable placement is: the ceiling line in AGENTS.md (it's a scope rule), and the granular deletion-test, edge-case, and test rules in `code-taste` and `spade-python-taste` — that way they fire at implementation time and again at the quality gate, and they cover agents that never read the global file's working-style prose closely.

Want me to apply that split in `~/.agents` and sync?

1	# AGENTS.md
2	
3	Global instructions for coding agents. Project-level `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`
4	files add local context and override only overlapping instructions.
5	
6	## Context Surfaces
7	
8	This machine has context tools that see more than the checkout in front of you.
9	
10	- **qmd** — search over ~12k local markdown docs: wikis, specs, past decisions,
11	  and session retros. For non-trivial work, run the `qmd-knowledge-base`
12	  preflight after identifying the repository and product area. Search when
13	  prior decisions, product intent, ownership, conventions, expected behavior,
14	  or known failures could change the correct solution; uncertainty is enough.
15	  Mechanical work fully defined by live source can proceed without it.
16	- **RepoPromptCE** — token-efficient codebase exploration: `file_search`,
17	  `get_file_tree`, `read_file`, `get_code_structure`, `context_builder`, and
18	  `manage_selection`. Beats `rg` plus file reads whenever the task spans more
19	  than a couple of already-known files. `context_builder` can build full
20	  implementation context for a task on its own. CLI fallback: `rpce-cli`.
21	- **`rg` and direct reads** — right for exact, small, already-located scopes.
22	
23	An answer, plan, or review that rests only on memory of the code is a guess.
24	Ground it on one of these surfaces first, and verify drift-prone details at the
25	live source.
26	
27	## Working Style
28	
29	- Work with a senior Design Engineer specializing in TypeScript and React.
30	- Aim for the smallest *resulting* system, not the smallest diff. Size is the
31	  essential complexity carried forward — concepts, indirection, special cases,
32	  total code — measured after the change, not the distance from the current
33	  shape. A refactor that removes more complexity than it adds is a smaller
34	  change than a one-line patch that props up a structure that should not exist.
35	- Treat the current shape as a candidate, not a constraint. Before patching, ask
36	  whether you would arrive at this structure building it fresh today. When the
37	  difficulty comes from the existing architecture, name replacing it as an
38	  option and surface the tradeoff — do not silently engineer around a shape that
39	  should be torn out.
40	- Wake up smarter than yesterday. Hold your own plan loosely: when new evidence
41	  shows the approach is wrong, back out the bad path and re-approach from the
42	  better structure rather than patching forward to protect work already done.
43	  Sunk effort is not a reason to ship a worse design.
44	- Understand the business reason before optimizing the code shape.
45	- Find root causes. Do not ship temporary fixes unless explicitly asked.
46	- Preserve local intent, naming, ownership boundaries, and file conventions in
47	  code you are not deliberately reshaping. Reshaping the structure that causes
48	  the problem is in scope; tidying neighboring code the task does not touch is
49	  not.
50	- Remove filler. Comments explain why, not what.
51	
52	## Communication Style
53	
54	- Use dyslexia-friendly formatting: lead with the answer, short sentences,
55	  short paragraphs, generous white space, one idea at a time.
56	- Use clear action headings such as `Fix now`, `Investigate`, and `Leave alone`
57	  when they make the answer easier to scan.
58	- Avoid walls of text, dense tables, long nested lists, and unexplained jargon.
59	- For code comments and other documentation, follow ASD-STE100 Simplified
60	  Technical English.
61	- Do not use “not just X, but Y” constructions. State the actual point directly.
62	
63	## Product Contract
64	
65	- For consequential or ambiguous requests, use the `prompt-check` skill to
66	  normalize the user's raw prompt before acting. See
67	  `skills/prompt-check/SKILL.md`.
68	- Before editing, identify the contract being changed: user action, UI state,
69	  backend payload, URL state, persisted state, rendered output, command behavior,
70	  or published artifact.
71	- Identify the owner boundary that should contain the change.
72	- Prove the changed contract at the closest real surface:
73	  - UI state and rendered output agree.
74	  - UI changes are checked in a real browser or local browser automation when a
75	    route, story, or preview surface exists.
76	  - Backend and request contracts are exercised with real or representative data.
77	  - Docs are updated in the canonical destination and read back.
78	  - Touched files are clean for relevant lint, format, type, test, and
79	    applicable taste-skill gates.
80	- State what was proven and what was not. Do not let passing commands stand in
81	  for user-facing verification.
82	
83	## Scope
84	
85	- Completeness means fully solving the accepted product contract, not expanding
86	  the contract.
87	- Boil the ocean inside the agreed boundary: finish the accepted task, with tests
88	  and proof, without drifting into neighboring workflows.
89	- Do not improve adjacent UX, focus behavior, validation, styling, data modeling,
90	  persistence, or ownership boundaries unless the user explicitly asks or the
91	  accepted contract cannot work without it.
92	
93	## Code Shape
94	
95	For TypeScript and React code — architecture boundaries, typed contracts,
96	helpers, effects, IO, testing seams — use the `code-taste` skill before
97	choosing an implementation approach. For Spade Python services, use
98	`spade-python-taste`. Those skills own the code-shape rules; this file does not
99	repeat them.
100	
101	## Non-Negotiables
102	
103	- For work associated with a Linear issue, retrieve and use Linear's exact
104	  branch name before editing. Rename the current branch if necessary; do not
105	  synthesize a replacement or keep an agent-generated branch name. If the exact
106	  Linear branch name is unavailable, ask before making changes.
107	- Never commit `.env`, secrets, API keys, credentials, or private tokens.
108	- Never push directly to `main` or `master`.
109	- Never delete, weaken, or skip tests to make a change pass.
110	- Never run destructive git commands or revert user changes unless explicitly
111	  asked.
112	- Run the relevant linter, type-checker, and tests before marking work done, or
113	  report the exact blocker and the narrower verification that passed.
114	
115	## Phase Skills
116	
117	Skill descriptions carry the when-to-use detail; this is the phase map:
118	
119	- Discover/context: `qmd-knowledge-base`, `ce-sessions`, `ce-slack-research`,
120	  `repoprompt`.
121	- Frame: `ce-brainstorm`; `ce-grill` for branchy or strategic ambiguity;
122	  `document-review` for requirements docs.
123	- Plan: `ce-plan`; `document-review` for markdown plans.
124	- Work: `ce-work`, then `ce-quality-gate`. Taste skills (`code-taste`,
125	  `spade-python-taste`) route code-shape decisions before implementation and
126	  are part of the completion gate for touched code; `frontend-design` for UI;
127	  `vercel-react-best-practices` for any React/Next change.
128	- Review: `ce-review`; `ce-simplify-code` for cleanup; `security-review` only
129	  for real trust-boundary asks.
130	- Ship/feedback: `git-commit`, `git-commit-push-pr`, `gh-fix-ci`,
131	  `resolve-pr-feedback`.
132	- Remember: `ce-compound` and `ce-compound-refresh` for durable `.ai`
133	  knowledge.
134	
135	## Task Artifacts
136	
137	- Keep generated agent artifacts under `.ai/`.
138	- Create durable todos or lesson notes only when the task genuinely needs them
139	  or a user correction reveals a repeatable pattern.
140	- For upstream instructions that mention bare `docs/` paths for agent artifacts,
141	  prefix them with `.ai/`.
142	- For docs, specs, research, and PR descriptions, identify the canonical
143	  publishing surface before editing. If Linear or GitHub is canonical, treat
144	  local markdown as the working copy and read back the published version.
145

2	name: code-taste
3	description: Apply TypeScript and React code-shape taste for implementation, review, refactor, and quality-gate tasks. Use when TypeScript or React changes involve typed contracts, helper boundaries, domain cores, IO or UI adapters, schemas, reducers, selectors, premature abstractions, speculative guards, maintainability smells, courier objects, JSX business logic, casts, useEffect, effect soup, or over-engineering.
4	---
5	
6	# Code Taste
7	
8	Use this skill for TypeScript and React architecture and code-shape judgment.
9	This skill is the single home for those rules; global `AGENTS.md` points here
10	and does not repeat them.
11	
12	## Authority
13	
14	- Follow local project conventions first.
15	- Follow explicit user instructions when they conflict with these defaults.
16	- Apply these rules harder to new code than to old code around it.
17	- Prefer the change that yields the smallest resulting system — least complexity
18	  carried forward — over the one with the smallest diff.
19	
20	## Routing
21	
22	For Spade Python-only changes, use `spade-python-taste` instead. Use both only
23	when the change crosses TypeScript or React and a Spade Python service.
24	
25	Use this skill before choosing the implementation approach. Do not save
26	code-shape thinking for the quality gate.
27	
28	- Load `vercel-react-best-practices` whenever a change touches React/Next
29	  rendering, data loading, effects, suspense, server/client boundaries, or
30	  bundle-affecting imports — even when the task is not framed as performance
31	  work. Match the change against its rule index and read the specific
32	  `rules/*.md` files that apply before implementing.
33	- Load `typescript-advanced-types` for real compile-time contract work:
34	  discriminated unions, generic APIs, schema inference, typed configuration.
35	- Skip supporting skills when the local convention already makes the right
36	  move obvious.
37	
38	## Architecture
39	
40	- Prefer contract-oriented code: a typed domain core with explicit IO, UI, and
41	  imperative-integration boundaries.
42	- Treat user actions, URL state, persisted state, backend payloads, mutations,
43	  subscriptions, cache invalidation, and rendered output as product contracts.
44	  Encode them with TypeScript types, schemas, endpoint metadata, discriminated
45	  unions, or explicit state-machine actions.
46	- Put deterministic behavior in named, typed, testable modules: schemas,
47	  parsers, reducers, selectors, validators, compilers, hydrators, adapters, and
48	  model helpers.
49	- Keep React components and hooks focused on rendering, user interaction,
50	  external subscriptions, IO coordination, cache coordination, navigation,
51	  analytics, dialogs, and imperative interop.
52	- Prefer compile-time guarantees over runtime checks when the type system can
53	  prevent the bug.
54	
55	## Smallest Change Bias
56	
57	"Smallest" means the smallest resulting system — least complexity carried
58	forward — not the smallest diff against the current shape. The bullets below
59	guard against over-building; the last guards against the opposite failure:
60	propping up a structure that should be replaced.
61	
62	- Prefer the direct edit that satisfies the current contract.
63	- Do not introduce a helper, wrapper, adapter, lookup, config layer, type guard,
64	  or defensive branch unless it removes current duplication, names a real
65	  invariant, crosses an actual runtime boundary, or makes the accepted behavior
66	  easier to prove.
67	- Do not hedge against hypothetical data shapes, impossible states, or future
68	  callers. If the product contract does not require the edge case and the current
69	  types exclude it, do not add code for it.
70	- Trust compiler inference inside typed code. Do not add casts, predicate
71	  helpers, or runtime checks to convince TypeScript of facts it can already know
72	  with clearer types or local narrowing.
73	- Parse or guard raw `unknown` data once at the external boundary, then pass
74	  typed values inward.
75	- Inline simple one-use logic unless extracting it makes the owner boundary,
76	  invariant, or test seam clearer.
77	- Do not prop up a shape that should be replaced. When a fix only fits by adding
78	  a special case, a flag, or a workaround to structure that is itself the
79	  problem, replacing that structure is the smaller change even when the diff is
80	  larger. Name it and surface the tradeoff rather than patching the local
81	  minimum.
82	
83	## TypeScript And React
84	
85	- Prefer `interface` for object shapes and `type` for unions, intersections, and
86	  utility types.
87	- Prefer React component function declarations with explicit return types when
88	  that fits the local style.
89	- Co-locate related component, hook, type, and test files when the project
90	  already uses that pattern.
91	- Name utilities as verb-based functions, then name the file after the main
92	  export.
93	- Use `unknown` plus parsing at external boundaries instead of trusting raw data.
94	- Avoid casts. If a cast is unavoidable, add a short `// SAFETY:` comment that
95	  explains the invariant.
96	- Hold `any` and `!` non-null assertions to the same bar: fix the type boundary
97	  or handle the null case. A genuinely unavoidable exception carries a
98	  `// SAFETY:` comment.
99	- Keep JSX from carrying business rules. Move shaping, validation, filtering,
100	  state transitions, and derived rows into helpers, selectors, reducers, schemas,
101	  adapters, or hooks.
102	
103	## Function Boundaries
104	
105	- Let broad workflow owners compose broad objects: public actions, render
106	  resolvers, validators, hooks, components, and IO adapters.
107	- Below that owner boundary, pass the smallest meaningful values a helper
108	  directly reasons about.
109	- Avoid courier arguments: broad objects passed through helper layers so a lower
110	  function can read one field or forward the object again.
111	- Avoid helpers that accept both a broad object and a value already derived from
112	  it.
113	- Broad objects are fine when the function truly owns a broad transition or
114	  invariant.
115	
116	```ts
117	const chartDateSetup = chartDefaultDateSetup(chart);
118	
119	return resolveTraceDateWindow({
120	  chartDateSetup,
121	  seriesDateSetup: series.dateSetup,
122	  traceWindow: trace.window,
123	});
124	```
125	
126	Prefer that over:
127	
128	```ts
129	return resolveTraceDateWindow(chart, series, trace);
130	```
131	
132	## IO And External Synchronization
133	
134	- Centralize fetches, saves, invalidation, and backend shaping behind query,
135	  mutation, command, or adapter hooks.
136	- Treat `useEffect` as a code smell for product/domain state, derivation, event
137	  handling, data loading, backend shaping, or parent-child synchronization.
138	- Before adding `useEffect`, exhaust event handlers, derived render values,
139	  reducers, selectors, query/mutation hooks, framework data APIs, refs, and
140	  explicit external subscriptions.
141	- Use `useEffect` only for synchronization with a real external system that no
142	  narrower framework or adapter boundary already owns.
143	- Isolate imperative engines behind controllers or adapters.
144	- Domain rules should return domain results. Callers own UI outcomes such as
145	  toasts, routing, dialogs, and analytics.
146	
147	```ts
148	type ValidationResult =
149	  | { ok: true }
150	  | { ok: false; reason: "duration-mismatch"; traceIds: string[] };
151	
152	function validateEqualDuration(spec: ChartSpec): ValidationResult {
153	  return hasEqualDuration(spec)
154	    ? { ok: true }
155	    : { ok: false, reason: "duration-mismatch", traceIds: traceIds(spec) };
156	}
157	```
158	
159	## Testing Taste
160	
161	- Test the lowest meaningful seam that proves the behavior: schema, parser,
162	  hydrator, reducer, selector, validator, URL sync, command, mutation, cache
163	  invalidation, hook, or adapter.
164	- Use component or browser tests when the regression is genuinely
165	  interaction-level, visual-state-level, or journey-level.
166	- Avoid render tests that only prove mocked wiring, prop forwarding, or effect
167	  calls.
168	- Prefer the project's existing test shape over a new harness.
169	
170	## Review Smells
171	
172	- JSX maps backend responses directly into UI rows.
173	- Helpers read only one or two fields from a broad object.
174	- A broad object is passed onward without meaningful local use.
175	- Derived values are recomputed after the caller already knows them.
176	- Effects coordinate state transitions that should be reducer actions.
177	- Fetch, save, invalidation, or parsing logic is scattered through components.
178	- A wrapper, lookup, adapter, or abstraction only packages a direct call.
179	- A helper exists mainly to hide a cast, type guard, or single property access.
180	- Runtime guards check states already excluded by the local TypeScript types.
181	- Defensive branches handle hypothetical edge cases outside the accepted
182	  contract.
183	- Tests mount UI just to observe mocked hooks.
184	- `useEffect` coordinates product state, mirrors props, loads data, shapes
185	  backend responses, or patches over ownership boundaries.
186	- Casts, `any`, non-null assertions, skipped tests, or ignored rules hide the
187	  real type or behavior boundary.
188
